The total of finite geometric external limits is presented, and a related computation theorem for these limits is formulated.  The theorem is applied to calculate the external limits of geometric totals for 3-dimensional ellipsoids when one dimension varies, and numerical results are obtained for external limits of totals when two dimensions are variable.

Tabular data representation is typically complex and noisy, comprising multiple numerical and categorical variables. Current models, such as linear and deep learning methods, are often insufficient in handling these challenges due to their inability to focus on specific rows and address noisiness. To overcome these limitations, we propose a new approach, known as SAINT, which involves row-focused attention and an enhanced pre-training method using the softmax dimension. This formulation is akin to the proxy contrastive learning method in self-supervised visual learning. To further improve the effectiveness of SAINT, we introduce a novel objective function that leverages the softmax dimension, leading to an enhanced contrastive loss. Through extensive testing on diverse real-world datasets, we demonstrate that SAINT surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both ranking and classification tasks. Moreover, our approach yields superior performance on open datasets, particularly in ranking tasks, and sets a new benchmark in classification tasks.

The conventional approach of deep learning with massive datasets is becoming impractical due to the high costs associated with data acquisition, especially in RF applications. A promising solution is to utilize transfer learning, which enables the use of pre-trained models in similar or related tasks with limited data. This study investigates the effectiveness of transfer learning in the context of RF signal detection. We present a novel synthetic dataset, designed to mimic the noise characteristics of actual RF signals, and employ it to train and test RF transfer learning models. The results demonstrate the potential of transfer learning in achieving high accuracy in detecting RF signals and reveal that the performance of these models is heavily dependent on the similarity between the source and target tasks.

The center vortex model's issue with Gribov copies can be addressed by redefining the model's core region concept. This redefinition involves considering the set of gauge function-defined gauge copies that remain invariant under gauge transformations that fix the boundary of a defined open set. The redefined concept leads to a reduced configuration space, $\mathcal{C}^*$, which has been shown to be Haag-Ruelle complete. Additionally, this new understanding of core regions enables the use of local field expansions, thus facilitating the incorporation of physical scattering processes into the center vortex model.

We've developed a new method for estimating the mass of compact dark matter sub-halos within localised galaxy clusters using data from the Dark Energy Survey. Our approach involves calculating the sub-halo mass based on the sub-halo's half-light radius, velocity dispersion, and the mass of the host cluster, and we've incorporated the effects of photoionization feedback to account for any dark matter destruction. Applying this method to a sample of 1432 low-surface-brightness galaxies with a range of redshifts (0.05-0.9) and various halo masses (10^11-10^15 solar masses) has allowed us to investigate the impact of photoionization on dark matter annihilation. Our findings indicate that the effect of dark matter destruction is relatively weak, with a 68% confidence upper limit on the photoionization mass fraction of 0.22. This suggests that the photoionization mass fraction is unlikely to be very high. Furthermore, our research reveals that the photoionization mass fraction is sensitive to the sub-halo's velocity dispersion, making it a useful tool for distinguishing between different dark matter profiles. We've also discovered that the photoionization mass fraction is not affected by the presence of a central supermassive black hole.

Our goal is to automatically modify search queries in order to uncover novel
concepts and refine information retrieval. To this end, we have developed SWIFTER,
a query rephasing system that utilises knowledge graphs to suggest new queries
tailored to specific information retrieval tasks. SWIFTER employs an unsupervised
approach, rephasing queries based on the occurrence of related entities within
a document and altering the query's keyword selection and order. Our platform,
built with an interactive UI, allows users to evaluate and refine its suggestions
in real-time. Our platform was tested by a large group of users who assessed the
effectiveness of SWIFTER's suggestions in identifying new entities related to their
search queries. SWIFTER outperformed a basic baseline method and demonstrated
promise in enhancing the precision of search results through dynamic query
rephasing.

We're focusing on efficient numerical solutions for a specific class of equations derived from modified Darcy equations, which describe the flow of multiple fluids within a porous media. Our approach involves a parameterized linear system, allowing for a family of matrices that vary based on a parameter. To develop a robust preconditioning technique, we utilize the low-rank property of this parameterized system, and demonstrate how a parameter-resilient method can be applied. The proposed method demonstrates the effectiveness of two LRC-based preconditioning strategies, allowing for a more accurate and efficient numerical solution. The comparative performance of these strategies is evaluated through a parameterized and non-parameterized framework, ultimately showing that a combination of the two approaches yields the most effective and robust numerical solution.

Generating concise and coherent summaries of extended conversations is a difficult task due to its structured and often disorganized nature. To address this challenge, our proposed approach utilizes a large dataset of annotated conversations to create summaries by first rearranging the conversation structure and then generating the summary. The primary innovation behind this two-stage method lies in employing a connection-based model to establish and visualize links between sentence pairs in different conversation segments, thus streamlining the summarization process. The outcomes of our experiments demonstrate the superiority of this approach over existing methods in evaluating the quality and coherence of summaries.

The use of machine learning in high-energy physics research has expanded significantly, particularly in analyzing Monte Carlo events. However, these models struggle to generalize when applied to real collision data due to the disparity between simulation and reality. A novel approach is proposed that incorporates a physically inspired deep neural network to predict the cross-section and correct for the distortions caused by Doppler widening in gamma-ray spectra resulting from astrophysical sources. The model was trained on simulated data generated by the PYTHIA8 Monte Carlo event generator and fine-tuned with data from the Fermi Large Area Telescope (Fermi-LAT). The model's accuracy in predicting the cross-section shows an improvement of 14% over a baseline calculation. Furthermore, it is shown that this model can effectively correct for the distortions caused by the detector.

This paper presents two primary objectives. The first objective is to develop the dendrification theory for $n$-Lie algebras, resulting in the creation of dendriform-$n$ Lie algebras. The second objective is focused on exploring $n$-pre-Lie algebras, specifically examining their connection to dendriform-$n$ Lie algebras and $n$-Lie groupoids. Additionally, key findings from these objectives are significant identities for $n$-Lie algebras, generalized Riccati equations, and solutions to the Yang-Baxter equation. The paper also includes an exploration of the relationship between $n$-pre-Lie algebras and color-$n$-Lie algebras, along with the introduction of the concept of color-$n$-pre-Lie algebras.

Cell-free massive MIMO systems are being considered a potential enabler for
the fifth-generation wireless technology.  One major challenge in cell-free
macy MIMO lies in designing its channel access control protocol.  This paper
takes advantage of the unique properties of cell-free massive MIMO to develop
a novel channel access control protocol called dynamic zone selection.  The
aim of this protocol is to meet diverse quality of service requirements across
different users.  It achieves this goal by dynamically allocating users to different
zones based on a technique called uplink multi-user detection, which considers
users' quality of service requirements and channel conditions.  The simulation
results demonstrate that dynamic zone selection can significantly enhance the
overall network performance, particularly when compared to static zone selection.
Furthermore, dynamic zone selection can significantly reduce the computational
overhead associated with uplink multi-user detection, making it a more efficient
option.

We establish a condition ensuring the convergence of the sequence obtained by repeatedly applying a single operator $A$ on an arbitrary vector, with the sequence starting from an initial vector not necessarily zero. The established condition is considered uniform convergence within the set of all possible initial vectors. This result is an extension of the well-known Theorem on uniform convergence of the sequence of powers of a single matrix, and generalizes the Weierstrass approximation theorem in a more versatile form.

The intricate relationship between a solid's static structure and its dynamic response is complex, yet understanding this connection is crucial for grasping the mechanical properties of solids. We have developed a computational method that can capture the average arrangement of a solid prior to a sudden deformation. By utilizing this approach, we can predict a solid's actual deformation when subjected to a mechanical stress. Our findings reveal a fundamental link between a solid's average pre-deformation arrangement and its resulting deformation, which is rooted in the memory of solid particles as they travel under stress. The arrangement of solid particles dictates the energy barriers that determine their subsequent motion, which in turn influences the development of stress and strain within the solid. This study provides a unified explanation for a wide range of mechanical phenomena in disordered solids, encompassing scenarios where energy barriers are high (such as in plastic deformation) or low (such as in compaction or shear banding).

The rapid development of object detection technology has significantly enhanced the capabilities of intelligent video analysis systems. Nevertheless, the existing solutions remain limited in addressing real-world applications involving continuous video streams. To further refine these technologies, an in-depth understanding of ongoing object detection is required, necessitating a comprehensive review of its core concepts, state-of-the-art methods, challenges, and relevant datasets. This critical examination aims to uncover the underlying principles and challenges in ongoing object detection, ultimately paving the way for research advancements in this field.

The BDMPS-Z formalism is employed to study the splitting of a hard gluon into two color charge dependent strings, which is a key process in understanding the medium-induced broadening of hard partons. We examine the resulting parton spectrum and its behavior in different color charge environments, comparing it to the established Langevin equation approach. The two methods are found to yield similar results for certain parameter ranges, which is consistent with previous findings for the case of vacuum-like splitting. The influence of the target's color charge is also considered and found to be relatively minor.

Deep learning's success in image classification has led to significant breakthroughs in many areas, but the lack of interpretability in these models hampers their use in high-stakes applications. To address this issue, researchers have developed new techniques that balance both accuracy and interpretability. In this study, we explore domain generalization in image classification, which allows models to achieve high accuracy without sacrificing interpretability, even when tested on data from unknown domains. To achieve this goal, we propose a new network structure called the Interpretable Domain Generalization Network (IDGN) that combines the benefits of classical neural networks and cutting-edge attention-based models. The IDGN architecture leverages attention to capture interpretable features from input images and demonstrates superior performance on multiple datasets compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

This paper introduces a communication system that enables agents to exchange information over limit domains of Internet infrastructure. Each agent is equipped with a blockchain that facilitates secure collaboration, trust establishment, and authentication. By leveraging the blockchain's decentralized consensus mechanism, the system addresses the significant security vulnerabilities arising from agents interacting over unsecured domains. To mitigate the inherent insights into communication that an opponent could gain by intercepting messages on these networks, the system implements a privacy-preserving protocol to safeguard message contents. Finally, the system's performance and efficiency are demonstrated through a simulation of blockchain-based inter-agent communication.

Our analysis focuses on the alpha-attraction model, a cosmological inflation model exhibiting natural flatness and a flat potential. By employing the slow-roll framework, we derive the key characteristics of the model, such as the number of e-folds and spectral indices. Furthermore, we explore how observational data influences our understanding of this model, leveraging Planck 2018 data for our analysis. We also extend our study to its natural supersymmetric counterpart and demonstrate that its predictions diverge from those of the standard model.

The widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) across various sectors has led to a growing demand for more efficient and accurate training and deployment processes. To meet this need, we propose a novel framework that integrates a range of optimization techniques for training and deploying AI models on a single server. This framework leverages the capabilities of Intel Xeon processors in conjunction with CUDA TensorRT for accelerated inference. Through extensive experimentation, we have identified and optimized hyperparameters such as batch size, learning rate, and momentum to achieve improved accuracy in vision and NLP tasks. Additionally, we have explored data augmentation techniques to enhance model performance and accuracy. Our results demonstrate that these optimization strategies enable models to achieve comparable accuracy with minimal training data, and in some cases, achieve higher accuracy with the same data.

A study by Linde et al. (2019) introduced a Bayesian approach to comparing paired values, which were later adapted by Vekberg (2020) to a frequentist framework. The original article by Linde et al. (2019) was subsequently re-examined by Reimann (2021) to establish a mathematical connection between the two formulations. This supplementary paper aims to demonstrate that the same equivalence can be achieved using different mathematical techniques, which were employed by Reimann (2021), but are also feasible with less sophisticated methods including algebraic manipulations and back-calculation.

In the realm of semantic transmission, we present a novel system, referred to as VQST, designed to transmit high-level semantic information at a rate comparable to that of a human context window. This new system leverages a trained VQ-VAE to capture the underlying distribution of an image database, and a VQ-Encoder to encode the target image into an encoded format. By sampling the VQ-VAE's latent space, we generate a set of possible vector quantization values, and a vector quantizer is utilized to determine the optimal quantized vector that best represents the encoded vector. This approach enables the VQ-Encoder to be eliminated, and the resulting feature map serves as the high-level semantic feature. This feature is then transmitted to the receiver, where it can be seamlessly integrated with any existing image database. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our VQST system, achieving comparable performance to that of a well-trained image encoder on a variety of image classification tasks, while also allowing for a dynamic database update.

This study addresses the ongoing obstacles in extracting meaningful insights from rapidly expanding amounts of data. We propose innovative BDA methods as practical solutions to these challenges. The proposed techniques aim to provide personalized analysis to users, optimizing their learning process and enabling the discovery of valuable results. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we present preliminary findings and examine their implications.

This work delves into the relationship between doctrines, universal constructions and comonads, with the main aim of providing a detailed explanation of doctrine as an abstract concept. A doctrine is essentially a mathematical framework comprised of a category paired with a collection of universal constructions that apply universally. Prior research has focused on doctrines within the context of string diagrams and functorial graph semantics, which also explored comonads as a particular instance of universal constructions. Although some studies have examined the relationship between doctrines and comonads, there is still a significant need for a thorough analysis of the connections between doctrines, universal constructions, and monads and comonads. This paper aims to address this gap in knowledge by integrating the existing research on this topic and presenting new insights.

A novel Bayesian nonparametric model, known as graphically assistant clustered network autoregression model (GACNAR), has been proposed for analyzing complex autoregressive network effects. GACNAR combines graph neural networks with Dirichlet process mixtures to capture network effects and cluster structures in large datasets from interconnected sources. This model introduces a clustering mechanism to the collective autoregressive model, allowing clustering variables into distinct groups based on their relationships. A Dirichlet process mixture is then used to determine the underlying clusters, while a graphical neural network identifies the connections between variables. A hierarchical Gibbs sampler is designed to simulate from the posterior distribution, allowing for model inference and cluster identification. A simulation study and a real-world case study on stock market relationships demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed GACNAR model.

A crucial component of many scientific evidence validation systems is determining whether a scientific hypothesis can be supported by individual evidence. This challenge involves comparing a hypothesis to various evidence, which is similar to the problem of comparing queries to text in open-domain question answering. Recent studies have shown that incorporating retrieval-based representations into claim validation systems is effective, but these representations are often expensive to compute and may not be suitable for use on a large number of evidence. This study introduces a new approach called RerrFact, which uses a single pass to reduce the complexity of evidence retrieval representation calculation. Specifically, RerrFact employs a two-stage approach that first uses a pre-trained BERT model to generate a hypothesis representation and a shared evidence representation, and then uses this shared representation to calculate the final evidence representation. The results of our experiments on two claim validation datasets reveal that RerrFact achieves comparable performance to a strong baseline while significantly reducing the computational cost.

A novel, automated approach is proposed for the detection and segmentation of posterior segment retinal diseases in OCT images. This method employs a multi-step process, beginning with a deep neural network that utilizes 2D convolutional filters to identify the presence of retinal detachment and segment the posterior segment. Building upon this initial detection, a second custom network is employed to precisely segment the retinal detachment within the identified region. Evaluation of the network's performance with a dataset of posterior segment OCT images yielded encouraging results, with a high level of agreement between the network's outputs and expert annotations.

The brain's ability to process information efficiently is achieved through a trade-off between the costs of cognitive processes and the benefits gained. This balance is reflected in the superstatistics model, which combines two key features: decision accuracy and the costs associated with evidence accumulation. By incorporating these elements, the model simulates how humans efficiently allocate resources to achieve optimal performance. However, the optimal strategies can change depending on the task, resulting in dynamic adjustments of cognitive processes. This research presents a new Bayesian framework, which allows for the estimation of cognitive strategies and their associated uncertainties. The method is applied to a wide range of accumulation-distribution tasks and demonstrates its superiority over traditional models, such as the drift-diffusion model, by accurately capturing the complexities of human behavior. The approach also reveals that humans efficiently allocate resources to achieve optimal performance in various tasks and the method provides a quantitative explanation for this efficiency.

This research paper introduces a groundbreaking approach for uncovering Mersenne primes utilizing the Gaussian elimination technique, yielding straightforward and efficient solutions. Notably, it demonstrates that its outcome is unique and efficient, and further, it has the potential to generate all Mersenne primes by iteratively adjusting certain coefficients. Additionally, we provide several concrete examples to illustrate the practical applications of this method.

Hilbert's sixth problem pertains to the general convergence of the Fourier transform of the velocity field within hydrodynamics. We will examine this challenge through the lens of exact and approximate partial differential equations governing the behavior of fluids. Our analysis will focus on the dynamics of collisionless plasmas, where the Vlasov-Poisson equation governs the behavior of the velocity field. We anticipate that the convergence of hydrodynamic structures will be influenced by the characteristics of the solutions to these equations, which are often non-linear and highly singular.

The molecular gas in galaxies can be characterized by the presence of subthermal stimulation in its magnetic fields, which may manifest as low-level fluctuations in C I lines. We have analyzed the C I lines 612.1 GHz and 609.3 GHz in M33 and M31, which revealed a relatively narrow line-of-sight velocity spread of 5-6 km/s. These findings suggest that the velocity spread is comparable to the width of the C I lines in the most dense regions of molecular clouds. We propose that the low velocity spread is due to the presence of subthermal stimulation, which is a common phenomenon in interstellar gas. This phenomenon may be observed in other interstellar gases, including neutral and ionized species.

This research paper outlines the creation of the first spoken language corpus for the Frisian language, utilizing DISCO format and UDS guidelines. A unique, code-switched dataset was chosen to reflect authentic spoken language use between Frisian and Dutch in bilingual households and public settings. The paper details the data collection process, annotation procedures, and existing challenges associated with spoken language treebanking.

The process of photoevaporation is a crucial factor in the development of protoplanetary disks and ultimately, the formation of planets. Research indicates that disk growth and evolution are significantly influenced by this process, but it is still unclear how photoevaporation is affected by various factors. A recent study has investigated how photoevaporation rates and lifetimes in disks are influenced by the mass of their host stars using a new, high-resolution model of their inner regions. By varying the mass of the central star, the authors have been able to accurately calculate the temperature and pressure profiles of the disk. Their results show that disk photoevaporation rates and lifetimes are directly related to the central star's mass. A 2-fold increase in the central star's mass results in a corresponding increase in the disk's photoevaporation rate and lifetime. The authors have also found that the disk's structure and the location of its evaporation radius change in response to the central star's mass. The new findings have implications for the development of planetary systems and the formation of giant planets.

This study introduces a set of explicit, high-order, and explicitly formulated methods for simulating structural dynamics using isogeometric analysis. The proposed methods are derived from well-established implicit time integration schemes, including the $\alpha$-Newmark, $\alpha$-Modified Newmark, $\beta$-Newmark, and Derivative-returned $\alpha$-Newmark. By reinterpreting these methods in an explicit framework, we gain a clearer understanding of their structure and the costs associated with each. We further enhance the methods' efficiency by integrating the following features: constant Jacobian matrix, absence of loops, and a simplified matrix factorization scheme. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through a set of numerical experiments, which show improved performance in terms of convergence, efficiency, and memory requirements, especially when employing the $\alpha$-Newmark and Derivative-returned $\alpha$-Newmark methods.

In a one-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensate with an attractive interaction and confined in a twin-well, a single impurity can form a stable polaron when its energy is below a critical threshold.  At higher energies above a threshold, the polaron decays rapidly due to the loss of its internal structure and this decay is studied in a numerical simulation.  The simulation shows that the polator's lifetime is influenced by its energy and the interaction between the particles and this interaction can be measured by analyzing the decay rate.  Specifically, the decay is found to occur in distinct phases, the first being a sudden loss of internal structure and the second being a gradual decay due to the loss of collective excitations.  The simulation also reveals that the decay can be suppressed by introducing an attractive interaction between the particles and this suppression can be used to investigate the polator's internal structure.

The provision of humanitarian, logistical, and medical services during a natural disaster is a critical component of disaster management efforts. This involves the coordination of numerous transportation vehicles to reach disaster-stricken areas, where the impact of recent climate change events has resulted in severe infrastructure damage. This complex problem is framed as a multi-phase network optimization challenge, where the goal is to minimize both costs and the time required to deliver essential resources. A novel, adaptive solution approach is proposed, where the method iteratively refines its strategy based on the results of previous operations. Initially, a probabilistic network model is developed to account for uncertain travel times and the impact of random events associated with disaster relief efforts. This probabilistic model is then translated into a deterministic format to facilitate the design of efficient, adaptive operational strategies. A computational study was conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, where the results were compared to a conventional, non-adaptive solution approach. The findings indicate that the adaptive method is capable of significantly reducing operational costs, improving performance reliability, and enhancing overall efficiency compared to traditional methods.

The precise timing of binary pulsar signal amplitudes is crucial for the aether-gravity experiment, which aims to detect gravitational waves. In order to improve the accuracy of the signal predictions, we have developed a new method that can accurately predict the timing of elliptical binary pulsar signals, taking into account various physical effects. This method can be used to study the orbital dynamics of binary pulsar systems and can be applied to current and future pulsar timing array data.

We're exploring the integration of human observation in continuous action-space environments for real-world applications and games. This study focuses on a novel game called Full Watched Chess. By leveraging advanced chess pieces with the ability to observe their opponents' moves, chess players must now balance their desire to protect their king with the need to outmaneuver their opponents' pieces. Through the application of the Win-or-Lose Monte-Carlo tree search algorithm, we've developed a framework that enables the evaluation of our new game against the standard chess variant. The results demonstrate that introducing watchability into chess significantly elevates its complexity by a factor of 40 to 50, making it more challenging for humans to master and requiring state-of-the-art AI algorithms to find optimal solutions.

The terahertz band is poised to revolutionize communication systems with its substantial data transfer speeds and precise capabilities.  However, the band faces significant obstacles due to its adverse weather conditions and difficulty in transmitting signals over long distances. To mitigate these issues, researchers are focusing on developing integrated photonics that combine optical and electronic components. Nevertheless, the technology is hindered by signal loss due to the absorption of light in materials. To address this, our study utilizes on-chip spectroscopy to study the absorption of water and air molecules in microfluidic channels embedded in silicon photonics. By analyzing the absorption of both low-loss air and high-loss water, we were able to determine the absorption coefficient of molecules in microfluidic channels. The findings suggest that the absorption of molecules in microfluidic channels is significantly lower than in more conventional waveguides, which could be attributed to the unique geometry of the microfluidic channels. The discovery has far-reaching implications for the development of integrated photonics and water-based photonic devices.

The COVID-19 pandemic has brought about a global health crisis, claiming the lives of millions and affecting hundreds of others. As researchers, the challenge now is to find a solution to mitigate its spread. To combat the virus, a proposed system, AIRSENSE-TO-ACT, utilizes artificial intelligence and multi-source data analysis to provide actionable data, alerting authorities to emerging hotspots, preventing new outbreaks, and ultimately lessening the impact of this health crisis. By integrating data from various sources, this system aims to provide precise insights into population behavior, identifying potential transmission risks and facilitating targeted interventions with greater accuracy. As a proactive tool, AIRSENSE-TO-ACT is designed to accelerate the recovery process, reducing the impact of this health crisis.

This paper introduces a multi-phase, fluid-structure interaction approach using
the smoothed particle hydrodism method, enabling the simulation of complex
interactions between solid and fluid components at different length scales.
To achieve this, the paper first outlines a method for multi-phase fluid dynamics
using SPH, followed by the description of algorithms for handling rigid particle
interactions and boundary conditions. Additionally, the paper presents a novel
technique for the dynamic simulation of solid structures using SPH-based finite
element analysis. Lastly, the paper's numerical methods are thoroughly evaluated
with a series of illustrative examples.

Nodal materials in real space are notable for their unique symmetry-protected states, which remain invariant under specific transformations. These states in the nodal surface in momentum space are also shielded by topological protection, yet exhibit distinct characteristics that are resistant to certain changes in the system. Recent advancements in realizing nodal surface states in photonic, phononic, and mechanical systems have garnered significant attention. This review delves into the fundamental principles and topological attributes of nodal surface states, including their resilience to scattering due to system symmetry. Furthermore, we outline distinct topological protection mechanisms applicable to nodal surface states in various physical systems and discuss experimental realizations of these concepts.

The HL-LHC computing facility, with an expected output of 15 pbit per year, will rely on the Guinevere simulation system to generate particle data used in offline analysis. With the current WPy8 job submission system, it is anticipated that the available computing resources will be insufficient to meet the anticipated demand by a margin of approximately 30%. In order to address this shortcoming, it is proposed to incorporate multiple event generator packages into the Guinevere simulation system.

The constant of proportionality between two means of positive numbers is referred to as a partial mean. We provide the definition of an invariant characteristic for partial means in the context of positive real numbers. Furthermore, we derive selected analytical results related to power means of higher order.

The process of star formation is significantly influenced by the material in the atomic and molecular forms found in interstellar space. The presence of molecular gas in the outer galaxy remains poorly understood, specifically in the Perseus arm where it was previously thought to be minimal. This study focuses on the location of the Perseus arm and the characteristics of molecular gas at this site. The analysis reveals a dense ring of molecular gas with a diameter of approximately 80 parsecs and a width of about 7 parsecs, located at a distance around 8 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. The mass of this ring is estimated to be about 1.1 million solar masses. The study also finds that the molecular gas in the Perseus arm is predominantly in the form of cold neutral neutral molecules and cold neutral hydrogen. The mass of this gas is estimated to be about 1.4 million solar masses. The study suggests that the molecular gas in the Perseus arm is a result of the interaction between the Perseus arm and the molecular gas in the molecular ring. The analysis of the molecular gas in the Perseus arm reveals a correlation with star formation, indicating that the molecular gas in the arm is a key factor in the star formation process.

This research paper examines how service costs impact the overall economy, using a unique framework that focuses on understanding the value of services in relation to their costs. By analyzing the demand for services and their production expenses, the model evaluates how different service levels affect the total income a person can earn. The results suggest that providing more services does not guarantee higher overall income unless other factors are considered, and the model also explores the implications of varying service costs.

Active matter systems exhibit complex behavior due to the interplay between their geometric structure and dynamic activity.  We investigate a three-dimensional active substance model comprising polar, disordered particles whose dynamics are influenced by the Peierls potential, using the Vitelli model.  To study this system's large-scale behavior, we employ a reduced hydrodynamics approach, focusing on the particle's collective motion, diffusion, and energy dissipation.  We observe that the active substance exhibits a stable, long-range-ordered nematic phase, characterized by a specific nematic order parameter.  Notably, this order parameter is directly related to the short-wavelength collective wave speed in the system, which is also influenced by the activity level.  Additionally, we demonstrate that the active substance's nematic phase is stable even in the presence of significant particle density fluctuations, and we examine the system's behavior under various conditions, including the absence of these fluctuations.  The outcomes of our study provide a deeper understanding of active liquid crystals and offer insights into the development of novel active materials.

Within the framework of a bag model, we investigate the doubly charmed baryon spectrum and corresponding semileptonic interactions. Our findings align with the experimental data on branching ratios, and we calculate the form factors for various transitions to determine the branching ratios. Notably, the doubly charmed baryon $\Xi_{c}^{+}$ is a promising candidate for explaining the recently discovered state by LHCb, and further analysis suggests that the states $\Xi_{cc}(3100)$ and $\Omega_{cc}(3000)$ have potential to confirm this hypothesis through specific semileptonic decay modes.

This study introduces a novel task called position embedding through
human-human embodiment dialogue, aiming to embed human positions on a map using
embodied dialogue for reference. To this end, we propose dialogue2pos, a
human-human dialogue positioning dataset, and a two-stage model, the visual- and
text-based components of which, refer to map images and dialogue transcripts
respectively. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this
two-stage model, achieving significant enhancement compared to a baseline method
and showing promising performance on real-world data. Our proposed model and
dataset will be made publicly available at an upcoming repository.

The analysis of rotating machinery vibrations is crucial for identifying potential failures. The use of spectral analysis to understand vibration frequency characteristics is beneficial, but it may be hindered by the challenge of selecting the correct frequency bands. This is particularly true when dealing with low signal-to-noise ratios, where incorrect feature extraction can lead to false diagnosis. This paper introduces a new method called Band Importance Factor (BIF) that assesses the significance of frequency bands. The BIF method utilizes a novel approach to evaluate frequency bands by comparing vibration frequency characteristics with a comprehensive rotating machinery dataset. The evaluation process involves a comprehensive assessment of dynamic characteristics, followed by the application of a sensitivity analysis to determine the importance of each band. The importance factor is then calculated to rank the frequency bands for analysis. This paper outlines the BIF method and demonstrates its effectiveness through an evaluation using a dataset from an industrial fan, showing its potential to improve the accuracy of fault diagnosis in rotating machinery.

The noncentrosymmetric superconductors CaTSi3, with T = Ir and Pt, were analyzed using muon spectroscopy to determine their ground state.  Muon spin spectroscopy results revealed temperature-dependent changes in the local magnetic field, indicating spin-triplet Cooper pairs.  Additionally, anisotropic zero-field muon-spin rotation spectra were observed for both materials, suggesting complex magnetic structures.  Temperature-dependent analyses of the muon-spin relaxation spectra for CaIrSi3 revealed a power-law relaxation, indicative of long-range order.  In contrast, the relaxation spectra for CaPtSi3 showed a distinct crossover from a power-law to a exponential decay, indicating the emergence of short-range magnetic correlations at low temperatures.  These findings, combined with the analysis of the muon-spin rotation and transverse-field muon-spin rotation spectra, suggest that CaTSi3 and CaPtSi3 are spin-triplet superconductors with triplet paramagnon modes, while CaPtSi3 also exhibits spin-density-wave-like magnetic correlations.

We introduce the Sparse Grid Traits Method, a numerical solution for solving Partial Differential Equations that have a continuous and once differentiable solution, demonstrating superiority over traditional methods. This innovative approach efficiently adapts to high dimensionality without significant computational expense, offering accuracy comparable to the multigrid method while outperforming it in large-scale cases.

Recent breakthroughs in quantum machine learning have demonstrated the potential
of quantum computers in tackling complex machine learning challenges. This study
investigates whether high-dimensional quantum computers can be utilized to achieve
advancements in existing quantum machine learning algorithms. We focus on a specific
problem known as quantum evaluation classification, where a quantum computer is tasked
with classifying high-dimensional quantum states. We identify a key distinction
between quantum machine learning and traditional machine learning, highlighting the
ability of quantum computers to utilize quantum data properties for classification. To
address this challenge, we propose a quantum algorithm that leverages the high
dimensionality of quantum data to achieve superior performance. We evaluate the
algorithm's efficacy through simulations of various quantum data distributions and
find that it can significantly outperform classical algorithms, particularly in
high-dimensional settings.

The integration of renewable energy and advancements in advanced automation technologies presents opportunities to significantly reduce carbon emissions across the energy sector.  However, these benefits can only be fully realized if systems operators effectively manage the complex interactions between various energy components.  We argue that successful integration necessitates a more comprehensive understanding of the interconnected dynamics of the energy sector, which currently remains poorly understood.  A new modeling framework is proposed to capture the complex interactions and dynamics of multiple energy systems, accounting for the influence of new energy technologies, and shedding light on the potential for substantial carbon reductions.  The framework's insights can inform the development of effective management strategies for systems operators.

The 2D filtration model is a versatile tool used to study the behavior of porous media by simulating the movement of fluid in a two-dimensional space. Over time, the model has been employed across multiple domains, including the assessment of oil spill dispersal, the prediction of groundwater contamination, the spread of pollutants in rivers, and the migration of inorganic compounds. This study demonstrates that machine learning algorithms can be leveraged to analyze the output of the 2D filtration model and generate novel insights based on simulated data. Specifically, this research demonstrates how machine learning can be used to identify the type of problem being solved, the underlying geometry of the model, and the location of fluid within the porous medium. Moreover, this research demonstrates that machine learning can be used to tackle problems that are difficult to solve using traditional computational methods, such as identifying the type of problem being solved.

In the past decade, significant advancements in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) have made it possible to capture images of individual gas and solid particles within a packed bed. This research focuses on a newly developed technique known as HyperMAPS, which uses Hyperpolarized Argon MRI to provide rapid, high-resolution images of a stationary bed's temperature distribution. This novel method enables researchers to obtain detailed temperature profiles and identify thermal gradients within the bed caused by gas phase heating. We have employed HyperMAPS to study temperature variations within a 10 cm high, 1.9 cm diameter bed, composed of 0.1 m.m. stainless steel particles, subjected to a gas temperature of approximately 40 degrees Celsius. The findings indicate a relatively low thermal gradient within the bed, and we have compared the measured temperature profiles with predictions generated by a previously proposed model for gas phase cooling in a packed bed.

In superconductors, thermal fluctuations can be considered an unconventional form of external force, distinct from magnetic fields, that can lead to the disruption of long-range order. Our research focuses on the phenomenon of 'doused' thermal fluctuations, characterized by their unpredictability and strong correlation with critical temperature. This type of thermal fluctuation can be effectively described by a thermal noise model, which is a stochastic extension of the Ginzburg-Landau equation. The thermal noise model can be used to derive a time-independent Fokker-Planck equation, which describes the evolution of the probability distribution function of the order parameter. The thermal noise model can be applied to various types of superconductors, including those with significant self-diffusion. The unpredictability of doused thermal fluctuations results in the enhancement of critical fluctuations, increased critical temperature, and a strong correlation between the order parameter and its corresponding noise. This correlation can be used to explain the reentrance phenomenon, which is observed in certain superconductors. The thermal noise model can be applied to the study of unconventional superconductors, including heavy fermions. As an example, we have applied the thermal noise model to the superconductor UTe$_2$, demonstrating that the reentrant superconductivity in this compound can be explained by the coexistence of superconductivity and a magnetic field.

This research utilizes deep reinforcement learning to automate radio link optimization for ultra-wideband communication systems. Deep Rl methods have been shown to effectively adjust network settings for such links, maximizing data throughput. In this work, we apply deep reinforcement learning to adjust the radio configurations of UWB links in real-time, based on evolving channel conditions. Our approach involves training a deep Rl agent to make optimal adjustments, including sampling, power control, and rate setting, across various UWB links. Our simulation results demonstrate that this agent achieves a 10% increase in data throughput compared to manual adjustment.

We investigate the $k$-median clustering problem in metric spaces, particularly under Fr\'echet and Hausdorff distance constraints on input data points. We demonstrate that in the context of a bounded distance metric $d$, the difference in cost between an optimal solution and an $\epsilon$-optimal solution is bounded by a value that depends on the chosen norm (e.g. $\ell_2$ or $\ell_\infty$) and grows polynomially with $\epsilon^{-1}$ but logarithmically with respect to $d. This result has implications for approximation algorithms and suggests that in such metric spaces, the $k$-median problem can be approximated up to a constant factor by using a simple greedy algorithm. This contrasts with unbounded distance metrics, where a logarithmic dependence on $d$ may occur. Our findings are the first to establish such bounds for the $k$-median problem under Fr\'echet and Hausdorff distance constraints, and the first to show that in bounded distance metrics, the $k$-median problem is approximable within a constant factor.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) methods based on policy iteration have gained popularity due to their ability to achieve stable convergence within decentralized settings. However, these methods often fall short of achieving efficient convergence due to the complex interaction between agents and the high computational cost of policy evaluation. To overcome these limitations, a new approach is proposed, which uses subgradient and linear minimization in a decentralized primal-dual optimization framework. This method enables the development of a faster and more efficient policy iteration algorithm, termed MADDPG, which achieves significant improvement in sample complexity and convergence speed. Moreover, MADDPG maintains the consistency and optimality of the proposed policy, which are critical factors in reinforcement learning. In addition, MADDPG provides theoretical guarantees for the convergence and stability of the learning process. Experimental results on StarCraft II benchmark tasks demonstrate that MADDPG outperforms existing MARL methods in terms of sample efficiency and policy evaluation speed.

We establish a coalgebraic verification framework for the $\mu$-calculi of stochastic, imperative, and imperative probability processes. This framework enables the use of coalgebraic reasoning to determine whether program paths conform to specification sets, based on deterministic and monotone constraints. A novel coalgebraic soundness argument is provided, leveraging a Galois connection between Moore and coalgebraic predicate liftings. Furthermore, the results are leveraged to develop a coalgebraic verification tool for the functional arithmetic $\mu$-calculus, capable of verifying the correctness of specification-satisfying program paths.

We propose a novel reconstruction technique that utilizes Isogeometric Analysis (IGA) and reduced-rank tensor (RRT) estimation to reconstruct sparse initial conditions for partial differential equations. IGA allows for the use of various basis functions, which can capture initial patterns in solutions. However, it may not efficiently reconstruct sparse data due to its high regularity requirements. Our approach leverages the flexibility of IGA to choose suitable spaces and the sparsity of initial data to reconstruct initial conditions using low-rank and low-sparse RRT. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a single-component Burgers equation and the two-component Euler equations, highlighting its ability to accurately reconstruct the initial conditions with significantly fewer non-zero elements.

The rapid growth of vehicle-related technology is currently outpacing the development of infrastructure, necessitating the use of shared resources such as roads and sidewalks.  As a result, the potential for collisions between vehicles and pedestrians is escalating, prompting the need to create a more comprehensive and accurate mapping of urban environments to prevent accidents.  A new approach to achieving this goal involves leveraging vehicle-tracking data and mapping algorithms to create detailed, three-dimensional representations of indoor and outdoor locations.  By incorporating this data into a city map, the location of air conditioning, heating, and ventilation facilities can be identified, enabling the generation of predictive models for indoor climate conditions.  The proposed system utilizes this information to create highly accurate maps of indoor air quality and temperature, offering valuable insights for optimizing indoor comfort levels.

We've developed a representation of the generalized special linear group $G$ over the ring $R$ consisting of cut polynomials over a finite field ${\mathbb F}_q$, where $G$ is associated with a second-class involution $\sigma$ that satisfies specific conditions. This allows us to study the Weil representation of the double covering of $G$, denoted $\widetilde{G}$, without first constructing the corresponding Weil representation for $G$. Our approach yields the first instance of a Weil representation for a group of this type. Additionally, we utilize the representation to investigate the automorphism group of a covering group $\widetilde{G}^{+}$ that naturally arises from $\widetilde{G}$.

Considerable advancements have been made in producing high-quality, realistic, and engaging video content. Given the growing demand for engaging media in multiple fields, an increasing number of researchers are working to enhance video authenticity and visual appeal. Video manipulation can be categorized into two primary forms: authentic (e.g., applying filters, stylizing video) and fake (e.g., deepfakes, video forgery), with a focus on the second type in this study. Realistic, yet misleading video generation poses a significant threat to society, necessitating a review of its potential risks and an examination of the latest advancements in this area. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the fake category, with a focus on its applications, the latest methods, and the associated challenges. Furthermore, we discuss potential solutions and future directions for advanced fake video synthesis.

We introduce a novel approach to create a compact representation of charged particles within spatial traps. By extending a classical method for balancing particles, we derived a set of ordinary differential equations governing the motion of particles in the given traps. Subsequently, we apply this framework to investigate the dynamics of particles confined in linear and triangular quadrupole fields and confirm the existence of compressed coherent states. Furthermore, we experimentally demonstrate the observation of these compressed states in 40Ca+ ions confined in a linear Paul trap and hexapole ion trap, and our findings are consistent with theoretical predictions.

In the life sciences, simulations of cellular and tissue processes are crucial for understanding living systems through the development of computational models. By using these models, researchers can simulate and analyze experimental findings to gain insights into the mechanisms underlying biological phenomena. However, developing these models involves selecting various parameters, the values of which are often not known, and adjusting them to match experimental data. This process can be both time-consuming and require a deep understanding of the biological system in question. This study proposes a novel approach that leverages the potential of high-performance computing systems, combined with machine learning techniques, to automate the process of selecting the best possible model parameters. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by successfully applying it to a specific model of neuronal activity, allowing us to identify the best fitting parameters using a limited number of computational resources.

This paper presents a unique dataset collection known as Concealed Instance Segmentation (CIS) that consists of natural images with objects partially hidden by other entities within a scene. To address CIS, a new segmentation approach called Instance Concealment Network (ICN) is introduced, which utilizes a two-stage framework to identify and conceal objects. The first stage involves object concealment, where the network conceals identified objects using geometric models of concealment. Next, the second stage refines the concealment areas through iterative refinement. To evaluate the performance of CIS, various baseline methods were developed and compared using the proposed CIS dataset, with results indicating that existing segmentation methods are severely limited by the CIS domain. To bridge this knowledge gap, a comprehensive benchmark suite for CIS is established to facilitate fair evaluation of segmentation methods in the concealed domain. The source code, benchmark suite, and dataset can be found at the following link: https://github.com/zhonggecui/CIS

In our research, we explore how violating special relativity affects the superconducting transition temperature $T_c$ and superconducting density of states. By employing a BCS-like model, we find that modifying the energy- and momentum-dependent coupling force between electrons can be achieved through a dimensionful coupling to an effective field theory. This new coupling, denoted as $\mathcal{L}$, is proportional to the square of the Lorentz factor $\gamma$. Upon evaluating the impact of this modification on $T_c$ and density of states, we discover that, under certain conditions, modifying the Fermi-Dirac distribution with $\gamma^2$ leads to $T_c$ decreasing with $\gamma^2$ but remains finite as $\gamma$ approaches infinity. Conversely, the leading contribution to the density of states remains unchanged for $\gamma<5$.

As AI technology advances, its reliability and transparency have become increasingly pressing concerns. We have developed an innovative method to identify and report AI errors through crowd-sourced reporting, where human crowdworkers document specific instances of AI malfunction. We have created an intuitive interface for reporting these errors and a system to categorize and validate these reports. The system has been tested with a language model and an image classifier. The results show that human observers are able to detect AI errors more effectively than automated tools, providing valuable feedback that helps developers to address and improve their models. We have found that reporting AI errors can be used to create a "bug report map" that reveals the specific scenarios in which an AI system malfunctions, allowing developers to take corrective action. The study demonstrates the benefits of crowd-sourced reporting in revealing AI errors and facilitating the improvement of AI models.

Object detection in complex, cluttered environments poses significant challenges to deep neural networks. To enhance their performance, a novel approach called stochastic decision routing has been developed, offering an effective solution. SDR empowers neural networks to simultaneously predict multiple feasible object positions, then adaptively select the best one based on instance counts. By doing so, networks like YOLOv4 and Swin Transformer can significantly reduce spurious predictions and boost overall accuracy. The benefits of SDR have been consistently demonstrated in diverse scenarios, including object detection, semantic segmentation, and semantic routing, resulting in substantial improvements. The accompanying code is available at https://github.com/zhaiyiduan/SDR.

Recent studies have shown that FGSM adversarial training can lead to significant overfitting when defending against this type of attack. This paper proposes a method to mitigate this issue, which involves restricting the model's ability to focus on features that are easily affected by noise. This is achieved by minimizing the gradient of the loss function on clean data with respect to the feature vector, which helps to minimize the impact of noise on the predictions made by the model. This method has been shown to effectively reduce overfitting and improve accuracy on the WGAN-CIFAR10 dataset. Furthermore, it has been found that FGSM adversarial training can be effective in preventing overfitting even when using a large number of training examples.

Recent findings suggest that a specific type of cosmological black hole metric, known as the "Thakurta metric," is invalid. This metric, initially proposed in 2015 for black holes formed during the radiation-dominated era, was based on an assumption that their horizon could be in a state of negative mass flux. This assumption, however, is contradicted by a more recent and physically consistent model of these black holes that does not exhibit the Thakurta metric. Consequently, the Thakurta metric's absence does not impact existing limits on Planck-scale black hole production in cosmology or their contribution to the present-day density of the universe.

This research paper investigates how variations in online portfolio diversification impact the efficiency of leading hybrid optimization algorithms, including those based on the Pattern Search and Adaptive Simulated Annealing methods. To evaluate the effects of different diversification intervals, the authors conducted a thorough analysis on a set of benchmark problems, comparing the results across three distinct continuity levels and three different optimization algorithms. The findings reveal that, while there is no one-size-fits-all approach to continuity and algorithm selection, a general guideline exists. Specifically, a short continuity period tends to yield optimal results for problems characterized by low complexity, while a longer continuity duration is suitable for more intricate problems. The study further examines how the choice of algorithm influences performance, demonstrating that, for problems with low complexity, local search algorithms like PSO show remarkable resilience to variations in continuity. Conversely, problems with high complexity demand the use of metaheuristics like ASA for optimal results.

A fully homomorphic encryption scheme enables data encryption and decryption of any computation result. However, currently implemented schemes, although theoretically possible, are vulnerable to cyber-attacks due to the need for large key sizes, slow homomorphic computation, and extensive memory requirements. In this paper, a novel approach, called a homomorphic encryption bootstrapping catalyst (BTS), addresses these limitations by introducing a new EFF (encrypted for encryption) gate. The new gate enables the use of smaller key sizes, allowing for faster and more efficient computations. Additionally, BTS reduces the memory requirements of the entire system and enables the implementation of NAND gates with a lower time complexity of O(n) and O(m).

We present a collection of solvable random matrix models featuring logarithmic
confining potentials, broadening the scope of harmonic oscillator and Gauss-Hermite
known results. We establish the large N limit of these random matrix models within
the N-phase space, employing N x N Hermitian matrix realizations.

Our experiments have found a way to create entangled states between two distinct parts of a 3-level atom system using laser pulses. These entangled states are stable and can be used to represent quantum connections. We discovered that the duration of the entangled states is influenced by the strength of the atom's internal connection, as described by its gyration parameter. Additionally, the experiment showed that the entangled states can be transferred between different parts of the atom system and that the process of applying a specific light pattern can induce simulated quantum motion, mimicking the behavior of particles with mass.

In the context of a broader class of theories that incorporate Bell's theorem conditions, we establish a new concept of state locality, building upon the idea of spatial locality. This development introduces a new aspect, dubbed causal locality, which enables us to define state decomposability in these theories. Notably, our method yields a more efficient and straightforward test of Bell's theorem than the original inequality. However, our analysis indicates that the initial formulation of Bell's theorem conditions actually guarantee the existence of a pure state in these theories; indeed, causality becomes essential in this process, underscoring the need for a more comprehensive understanding of nonlocality.

We introduce StyleGAN-V, a versatile video generation tool that surpasses the performance of GAN-related methods, including Vid2Vid and VidGen, in multiple aspects. Unlike existing video generation algorithms, StyleGAN-V utilizes a single, continuous generator for video creation, allowing for more efficient and scalable production. By leveraging the capabilities of StyleGAN2, StyleGAN-V not only generates high-quality videos but also learns the temporal dynamics of training samples. To facilitate large-scale video production, we develop a method for accelerating video generation speed by a factor of three to four. Our evaluation indicates that StyleGAN-V produces videos of equivalent quality to existing approaches while requiring significantly less memory and processing power.

We explore discrepancies in degrees for elements of the monogenic image part of small degree points in eta correspondence under both the standard and twisted 2-modular representations for the degree 3-16 and 3-17 eta correlations.

Dosimetry techniques involving luminescence detectors are widely used in various fields such as medical dosimetry, radiation protection, and security. The accuracy of dose measurements obtained through luminescence techniques is crucial in high-stakes applications. Researchers have recently developed a new deep learning-based method to improve dose estimation, which leverages the TL signal's unique characteristics including its temporal pattern and duration after exposure. The proposed method utilizes two types of recurrent neural networks: long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent unit (GRU) models. These models were trained on actual human irradiation data and demonstrated improved dose estimation, particularly in low-dose scenarios. The proposed method was also compared to alternative approaches, including Gaussian mixture models and the widely used TL-Score method. The results showed that the proposed deep learning-based method significantly outperforms these conventional methods.
